title: Listening Accuracy Handbook
subtitle: Stop losing easy marks in IELTS Listening
description: This handbook shows you how the four Listening sections work and how to avoid common mistakes with spelling, numbers and distractors. Each chapter gives you one practical skill and a short task to practise it.
audience: Bangladeshi learners at around Band 5 to 6 who understand much of the audio but lose marks through careless errors.

chapters.title: How the Four Sections Work
chapters.summary: Learn the shape of the Listening test so nothing surprises you on test day.
chapters.body:
The IELTS Listening test takes about 30 minutes and has 40 questions. There are four sections, and each section has 10 questions. You hear each recording once only. This one fact shapes everything in this book. You cannot go back, so you must be ready before the audio begins.

## The four sections
Each section has its own type of speaker and situation.

- Section 1: a conversation between two people in an everyday situation. For example, a student calls a language centre in Dhaka to ask about evening classes.
- Section 2: one person speaking about a social topic. For example, a guide describes the facilities at a community sports centre.
- Section 3: a conversation between up to four people in an education or training setting. For example, two students and a tutor discuss a group project.
- Section 4: one person giving a lecture on an academic subject.

The test usually becomes harder as it goes on. Section 1 is the most familiar and has the clearest speech. Section 4 has no break in the speaker, more complex ideas and more abstract language. Many learners at Band 5 to 6 collect most of their marks in Sections 1 and 2, then lose marks in Sections 3 and 4. Your plan is to protect the easy marks first and then grow in the harder sections.

## What helps you during the test
Before each section, you get time to look at the questions. Use all of it. Inside a section, the recording often pauses briefly between parts, and you can read the next group of questions then. The questions follow the order of the recording in most task types, so your answers arrive in the same order as the audio.

At the end, the paper-based test gives you 10 minutes to copy your answers onto the answer sheet. The computer-delivered test gives you about 2 minutes to check your answers. Know which format you will take, because your habits are different. On paper, you write on the question booklet while you listen and copy later. On computer, you type as you go.

## What costs marks
Three small things cost many learners marks that they actually earned.

- Wrong spelling. A correct idea with a wrong spelling is marked wrong.
- Going over the word limit. If the instruction says NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS, three words is wrong.
- Losing your place. If you stay thinking about question 4, you will miss question 5 and 6.

Tip: When you lose your place, let the missed question go. Find the next question in the recording and keep going. One lost mark is better than three.

## How to use this book
Each chapter teaches one skill and ends with a short self-check task. Do the task before you move on. Practise with real test audio where possible, but also practise by listening to short clips of English every day, such as news, podcasts or lectures with transcripts.

Example: Rahim listens to a Section 2 recording about a city bus service. He reads the questions first and sees that the answers are about routes and timings. When the speaker says "the 42 now runs every fifteen minutes", he is already waiting for a number, so he catches it easily.

Good listening is not magic. It is preparation, attention and clear habits. The next six chapters build those habits one at a time.
takeaways: Listening has 4 sections, 10 questions each, 40 in total, and the audio plays once.
Sections get harder: protect easy marks in 1 and 2, then build 3 and 4.
Spelling and word limits are marked, so small errors cost real marks.
If you lose your place, let one question go and rejoin the audio.
chapters.exercise: Write the four sections from memory with one example situation for each. Then check which section you usually find hardest and say why in one sentence.

chapters.title: Predict Before the Audio Starts
chapters.summary: Use the reading time to guess the type of answer, so your ears know what to catch.
chapters.body:
Good listeners are not just waiting. They are already expecting something. Before each recording, you have time to read the questions. This time is the most valuable part of the test. If you spend it well, the audio feels slower and clearer.

## Read the instructions first
Always read the instruction line carefully. It tells you the word limit, such as NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER. It also tells you the task type. If you ignore it, you may write correct words that still get no mark.

## Predict the type of answer
For each gap or question, ask yourself one simple question: what kind of word is missing? Then decide on a category.

- A number: a price, a date, a phone number, a quantity.
- A name: a person, a street, a place.
- A noun: an object, a subject, a job.
- An adjective: a description, such as "quiet" or "expensive".
- A time or day.

Look at this note: "The class starts at ____ on Saturday." You know the answer is a time. Now, when you hear "half past six", you can write 6.30 at once. You also know that you must be careful about 6.15 and 6.50, because speakers often change a time.

Example: A form says "Name of hotel: ____". You predict a proper name. Then you listen for a capital-letter word, perhaps spelled out. You will not waste attention on other words.

## Underline keywords
Underline two or three keywords in each question. Keywords are words that carry the meaning, such as "cheapest", "only on weekends" or "main problem". The speaker will usually say these ideas in different words. If the question says "cheap", you may hear "good value" or "doesn't cost much". Train your ear for meaning, not only for exact words.

## Use the pause between parts
In the recording, there is often a short pause before a new group of questions. In that pause, do not look back at the last question. Look forward. Read the next group, underline keywords and predict again. Learners who look back lose the start of the next part.

Tip: Draw a small arrow in the margin when you are ready for the next part. It reminds you to keep moving forward.

## Watch the speaker's signals
Speakers give signals before important information. Words like "however", "actually", "in fact", "but" and "the main thing is" often mean that a correction or the real answer is coming. If a speaker says "We open at nine... actually, from this month, it's eight thirty", the answer is eight thirty.

## Practise prediction without audio
You can train this skill at home. Take a Listening task from a practice book. Do not play the audio. Read the questions and write your prediction for every gap. Then play the audio and check how many predictions were right. Do not worry if many are wrong at first. The goal is to build a habit of expecting information.

Prediction does not mean forcing your guess into the gap. If the audio says something different, trust the audio. Prediction prepares your ears. It does not replace listening.
takeaways: Use all the reading time and read the instruction line for word limits.
Decide the type of answer for each gap: number, name, noun, adjective or time.
Underline two or three keywords and expect different words with the same meaning.
Look forward during pauses and listen for signals like however and actually.
chapters.exercise: Take any 10 Listening questions from a practice book. Without playing the audio, write the answer type for each gap, then play it and count your correct predictions.

chapters.title: Spelling and Number Traps
chapters.summary: Avoid the small mistakes with letters, numbers, dates and plurals that lose easy marks.
chapters.body:
Many learners understand the recording but still lose marks because of the way they write the answer. This chapter helps you protect marks that you have already earned with your ears.

## Spelling counts
In IELTS Listening, a wrong spelling is a wrong answer. Both British and American spelling are accepted, but you must be consistent in a single answer. For example, "colour" and "color" are both fine. Write clearly in capital letters on the answer sheet if your handwriting is hard to read.

Learn the spellings of common words that appear again and again.

- Days and months: Wednesday, February, Thursday, August.
- Everyday nouns: accommodation, address, library, equipment, environment.
- Course words: schedule, assignment, deadline, laboratory, department.

Keep a personal list of words you misspelled in practice. Review it every week. Ten minutes of review is more useful than an hour of random practice.

## Letters spelled out
In Section 1, speakers often spell a name. The danger is letter sounds that are close. Many Bangladeshi learners mix up these pairs:

- A and E, and also E and I
- B and V, and also P and B
- G and J
- M and N
- S and F

Practise the alphabet aloud in English every day. Then practise with a friend who spells names slowly while you write them. Also remember double letters. When you hear "double L", write LL. When you hear "W as in water", the second part only helps you check the letter.

## Number traps
Numbers are easy to hear and easy to mix.

- Thirteen and thirty, fourteen and forty, fifteen and fifty. In the first word, the stress is on the end ("thir-TEEN"). In the second, the stress is on the start ("THIR-ty").
- Phone numbers are read in small groups. "Double five" means 55. "Oh" means zero.
- Years are usually read in two parts: "twenty twenty-five" is 2025.
- Prices: "two fifty" can mean 2.50. Pay attention to the currency in the question.

Example: You hear "The deposit is forty pounds, no, sorry, fourteen pounds." The final number is the answer. Speakers correct themselves often, so wait until the speaker has finished.

## Dates and times
Dates may come as "the third of May" or "May the third". You can write 3 May or May 3, and both are accepted if clear. Check whether the question wants a month or a full date. Watch for "half past", "quarter to" and "twenty to" in times. Write the time carefully, such as 9.45.

## Plurals and small endings
If the question needs "buses" and you write "bus", you may lose the mark. Listen for the final s sound. When the sentence before the gap says "two", the answer is probably plural. Also, check articles and grammar around the gap. If the note says "a ____", the answer begins with a consonant sound or a general noun.

Tip: In your last minutes of checking, do not change a right answer to a guess. Check spelling, plurals and word limits only.
takeaways: Wrong spelling is a wrong answer, so keep a personal list of mistakes.
Practise letter pairs that sound close, and note double letters.
Listen for stress to separate numbers like fifteen and fifty.
Wait for self-corrections and check plurals and word limits before you finish.
chapters.exercise: Ask a friend to read ten names, five phone numbers and five dates to you slowly. Write them down and check your accuracy. Note the letters or numbers you mixed.

chapters.title: Form and Note Completion
chapters.summary: Fill gaps in forms, notes and tables with the exact words from the recording.
chapters.body:
Form, note, table, flow-chart and summary completion are among the most common task types in Listening. They look simple, but they punish careless habits. In these tasks, you write words you actually hear, and the words must fit the gap in meaning, grammar and length.

## Understand the layout first
A form, such as a booking form, asks for details like name, date, address and phone number. Notes are shorter and often have headings. A table has rows and columns, and you should know which column the answer belongs to. Spend your reading time on the layout. If you know the headings, you know what kind of information will appear.

## Follow the order
The answers come in the same order as the questions. When you hear the speaker finish one idea and start another, you should be moving to the next gap. Do not wait for a perfect hearing. If you are unsure, write your best attempt and move on.

## Use words from the audio
You must use the words you hear. Do not change the form of a word unless the grammar demands it. If the speaker says "It's on the second floor", and the note says "Location: ____ floor", you write "second". Do not write "2nd" if you were not sure it is accepted; the safest answer is the word that you heard.

Check the word limit before you write. If the limit is ONE WORD ONLY, a phrase like "student card" is wrong. A hyphenated word such as "check-in" usually counts as one word, but do not take a risk with it when a simpler single word is available. A number is a word under the instruction AND/OR A NUMBER.

## Check the grammar of the gap
Read the words before and after the gap. Ask what part of speech fits.

- "She works as a ____." A job or noun is needed.
- "The room is very ____." An adjective is needed.
- "They plan to ____ the report." A verb is needed.

If your answer does not fit the sentence, you have probably heard the wrong thing.

## Beware of distractors in forms
Speakers change their minds. Consider this example.

Example: The caller says, "I'd like the Tuesday class... oh, I work on Tuesdays. Can I do Thursday?" The answer is Thursday, not Tuesday. The first word you heard was a distractor.

Another common trap is the address. A speaker may say the street name, then spell it. Listen for the spelling, because it often differs from the English you expect. Dhaka-based learners should practise with Bangladeshi names too, such as Mirpur or Dhanmondi, since test speakers may give unusual place names that are spelled out.

## Tables and flow-charts
In a table, track the row and column. Mark the row you are listening to with your pen. In a flow-chart, the steps follow a sequence. Listen for sequence words such as "first", "then", "after that" and "finally".

Tip: If you miss an answer, do not stop. Write a quick guess in the gap and re-join the audio. You can often fix the gap later from the grammar.

## After the recording
Reread each answer in its sentence. Does it make sense? Is it spelled correctly? Is it within the word limit? These three checks take about thirty seconds and can save several marks.
takeaways: Study the layout and headings during reading time to predict the answer type.
Use the exact words you hear and respect the word limit.
Check the grammar before and after each gap.
Expect changes of mind: the final version is the answer.
chapters.exercise: Pick one completion task and, after finishing, check each answer for three things: word limit, spelling and grammar fit. Write down any answer that failed.

chapters.title: Map and Diagram Labelling
chapters.summary: Follow directions and descriptions to match places and parts with letters.
chapters.body:
Map and diagram tasks worry many learners because they ask you to listen and look at the same time. The good news is that the skill is learnable. You need three things: a clear picture of the map, a set of direction words and a calm way to follow the speaker.

## Look at the map before the audio
During reading time, do not just glance at the picture. Study it.

- Find the entrance or starting point. The speaker usually begins there.
- Note which way is north, if a compass is shown.
- Read the names of places already on the map. They are your landmarks.
- Look at the roads, rivers and paths. They show how the speaker will move.

Imagine you are standing at the starting point. Practise telling yourself how you would walk to each lettered place.

## Learn direction language
Maps use a small set of words again and again. Make sure you know all of them.

- Left, right, straight ahead, opposite, next to, beside, between, behind, in front of.
- On the corner of, at the end of, along, across from, past, just before.
- Up the stairs, on the ground floor, on the first floor.
- To the north, to the south, to the east, to the west of.

Be careful with "left" and "right". The speaker's left is not always yours. Usually, they describe the map as if you are walking through it. Listen for the phrase "as you walk in" or "facing the building".

Example: The speaker says, "Go past the library, and the cafeteria is on your right, just before the main gate." Find the library on the map. Walk past it. Look right. The place just before the gate is the cafeteria. You write the letter of that building.

## Follow, do not jump
Speakers follow a route. Keep your pen on the map and follow the route as they talk. If you hear a place name you do not know, do not worry. Use the landmarks. Many questions give you more than one clue, so a missed word does not mean a lost answer.

## Be ready for changes
As in other tasks, the speaker may correct a direction. "Turn left at the junction... actually, the path is closed, so go right." The final instruction is the answer. Also be careful of places that sound similar, such as "the gym" and "the game room".

## Diagrams and plans
A diagram might show a machine, a process or a building plan. Learn the names of parts before the audio. Predict what kind of word goes with each arrow. For labelling a plan, use the same method as a map. For a process, listen for the order of steps.

## Practise in daily life
You can build this skill every day. When you travel in Dhaka, describe the route in English in your head: "Turn left after the bus stop, then walk straight until the traffic signal." When you enter a new building, name the rooms and their positions. This builds the same language you hear in the test.

Tip: Use your pencil to mark each answer on the map as soon as you hear it, then move on. Do not wait until the end of the part.
takeaways: Study the map, entrance and landmarks during reading time.
Know direction words such as opposite, beside, past and across from.
Follow the route with your pen and listen for corrections.
Practise by describing real routes in English around your home.
chapters.exercise: Draw a simple map of your neighbourhood with five places. Write a short route description using at least six direction words, then read it aloud.

chapters.title: Multiple Choice and Distractors
chapters.summary: Choose the right option by listening for meaning and ignoring tempting wrong words.
chapters.body:
Multiple choice questions are not about finding a word you hear. They are about finding an idea that matches. This is a big mistake for many learners: they hear a word from option B and choose B immediately. Then they lose the mark, because the speaker mentioned that word only to reject it.

## Why distractors exist
Test writers include distractors on purpose. In a multiple choice question, all options are likely to be mentioned in the audio. Only one is correct. The others may be mentioned but then rejected, changed or applied to something else. The test is checking whether you understand the whole idea.

Example: The question asks, "Why did the student change her topic?" The options are A: it was too expensive, B: it was too difficult, C: there were too few sources. The speaker says, "At first, I thought it would cost too much, but the real problem was finding enough books and articles." The word "cost" matches A, but the real reason is C.

## A reliable method
1. Read the question and underline the keywords.
2. Read all options and underline the difference between them.
3. Listen for the exact point the question asks about.
4. Wait for the speaker to finish the idea before you choose.
5. Cross out options that are clearly rejected.

## Watch the signals of change
Distractors often appear before the signal word. Listen for words that show a change of mind.

- But, however, although, in fact, actually.
- At first... then, I used to... now.
- I thought... but it turned out.
- Not exactly, not really, not quite.

After these words, the true answer often follows.

## Paraphrase is the real skill
Options are usually paraphrases. They do not repeat the exact words from the recording. If the speaker says, "The lecture was so dull that I nearly fell asleep," the option might say, "The student found the lecture boring." Practise noticing meaning. When you review a practice test, compare each option to the transcript and write what the speaker said in different words.

## Questions with more than one answer
Some tasks ask you to choose two or three answers from a longer list. The same rules apply. The answers can come in any order, but the information usually appears in order in the recording. Mark each option with a tick, cross or question mark as you listen. Do not choose more answers than the question needs.

## Matching tasks
In matching, you connect items to a list of options, such as people and opinions. Read the list carefully so that you know the categories. Listen to who says what. The same person may express an opinion in several sentences, so wait for the final view.

## Keep calm
A multiple choice question can feel difficult because you read a lot in a short time. Do not read every option word by word. During the reading time, understand the main difference. Then use the audio to decide.

Tip: If you are unsure, pick the best option, mark it with a small question mark, and move on. Do not lose the next question for one hard one.

After the test, spend time on mistakes. For each wrong answer, ask: what distractor caught me? This turns every error into practice.
takeaways: Choose the idea that matches, not the word you recognise.
Expect all options to be mentioned and wait for the whole idea.
Listen for change signals such as but, however, at first and actually.
After each practice test, name the distractor that caught you.
chapters.exercise: Choose one multiple choice question you got wrong. Read the transcript and write one sentence explaining which words made the wrong option tempting.

chapters.title: Section 4 Lectures, Note-Taking and Your Revision Plan
chapters.summary: Follow a long academic talk, capture key words, and build a four-week practice routine.
chapters.body:
Section 4 is a lecture with no break in the speaker and no conversation to help you. It is the hardest section for most learners. But it is also very organised. A lecture has a structure, and if you follow it, the answers become much easier to catch.

## How a lecture is built
Most lectures have an introduction, several main points and a short ending. The speaker often tells you the plan: "Today I will talk about three causes of..." Use that. When you hear the plan, listen for the next point each time the speaker moves on.

Pay attention to signpost words.

- Sequence: first, second, next, finally.
- Contrast: on the other hand, however, in contrast.
- Cause and result: because of, as a result, this led to.
- Examples: for instance, such as, take the case of.

These words show you where you are in the talk.

## Notes that actually help
In Section 4 you usually fill gaps in a summary or notes, so you do not need to write full sentences. Instead, you listen for the key word that fills each gap. Still, short notes help in the harder moments.

- Write only key nouns, numbers and names.
- Use symbols and short forms, such as "&", "=", "up" and "down".
- Do not write full sentences.
- Keep your eyes on the next gap, not on your notes.

The most important rule: do not stop listening to finish writing. Write a word, and move on.

## Use the gaps as a map
The summary in front of you is a map of the lecture. The gaps are in order, and the sentences around them have the main idea. Read the text before the audio and ask: what is the topic, and what kind of word is missing? The lecture may use different wording, so listen for the meaning of the sentence.

Example: The summary says, "Heavy rain can cause ____ in low areas." During the lecture you hear "When rainfall is intense, low-lying neighbourhoods often suffer from flooding." The answer is "flooding". You can catch it because you predicted a result of rain.

## Build vocabulary for academic topics
Lectures cover subjects such as environment, history, technology, health and behaviour. Read short articles on these topics in English each week and keep a list of useful words. Listen to short talks, and read the transcript after.

## Your four-week revision plan
Use this simple routine. Adjust it to your timetable, including load-shedding or work hours.

- Week 1: Do one Section 1 and Section 2 task daily. Review every spelling and number mistake.
- Week 2: Add Section 3. Practise multiple choice and matching. Write down each distractor.
- Week 3: Focus on Section 4 and maps. Listen once, then check with the transcript.
- Week 4: Take two full timed tests. Practise copying answers carefully, as in the real test.

Each day, spend ten minutes on your mistake list. This is the most useful ten minutes of your practice.

Tip: Do not only count your score. Note why you lost each mark: spelling, number, distractor, lost place or unknown word. The reason tells you what to practise next.
takeaways: A lecture has a structure, so use signpost words to stay on track.
Take short notes with key nouns and numbers and keep listening.
Use the summary gaps as a map of the lecture.
Follow a four-week plan and review your mistake list every day.
chapters.exercise: Write your own four-week plan with the days and times you can really study. Add one rule for how you will record the reason for each lost mark.
